In [[topology]], a branch of [[mathematics]], a '''nilpotent space''', first defined by Emmanuel Dror Farjoun (1969),<ref>{{cite book|title=Homotopy Limits, Completions and Localizations|volume=304|series=Lecture Notes in Mathematics|first1=Aldridge K.|last1=Bousfield|author1-link=Aldridge Bousfield|first2=Daniel M.|last2=Kan|author2-link=Daniel Kan|publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]]|year=1987|isbn=9783540061052|page=59|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6Mw2plpWo2sC&pg=PA59 |doi=10.1007/978-3-540-38117-4|mr=0365573}}</ref> is a [[pointed space|based]] [[topological space]] <math>X</math> such that
* the [[fundamental group]] <math>\pi = \pi_1 (X)</math> is a [[nilpotent group]];
* <math>\pi</math> acts nilpotently<ref name=Dror71/> on the [[higher homotopy groups]] <math>\pi_i (X), i \ge 2</math>, i.e., there is a [[central series]] <math>\pi_i (X) = G^i_1 \triangleright G^i_2 \triangleright \dots \triangleright G^i_{n_i} = 1</math> such that the induced action of <math>\pi</math> on the quotient group <math>G^i_k/G^i_{k+1}</math> is trivial for all <math>k</math>.

[[Simply connected space]]s and [[simple space]]s are (trivial) examples of nilpotent spaces; other examples are connected [[loop space]]s. The [[homotopy fiber]] of any map between nilpotent spaces is a disjoint union of nilpotent spaces. Moreover, the null component of the pointed mapping space <math>\operatorname{Map}_*(K,X)</math>, where <math>K</math> is a pointed, finite-dimensional [[CW complex]] and <math>X</math> is any pointed space, is a nilpotent space. The odd-dimensional real projective spaces are nilpotent spaces, while the projective plane is not.

A basic theorem about nilpotent spaces<ref name=Dror71>{{Cite book|last=Dror|first=Emmanuel|date=1971|contribution=A generalization of the Whitehead theorem|title=Symposium on Algebraic Topology (Battelle Seattle Res. Center, Seattle, Wash., 1971)|publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]]|series=[[Lecture Notes in Mathematics]]|volume=249 |pages=13–22 |doi=10.1007/BFb0060891 |isbn=978-3-540-37082-6|mr=0350725}}</ref> states that any  map that induces an integral homology isomorphism between two nilpotent space is a weak homotopy equivalence. For simply connected spaces, this theorem recovers a well-known corollary to the [[Whitehead theorem|Whitehead]] and [[Hurewicz theorem|Hurewicz]] theorems.

Nilpotent spaces are of great interest in [[rational homotopy theory]], because most constructions applicable to simply connected spaces can be extended to nilpotent spaces. The Bousfield–Kan nilpotent completion of a space associates with any connected pointed space <math>X</math> a universal space <math>\widehat{X}</math>  through which any map of <math>X</math> to a nilpotent space <math>N</math> factors uniquely up to a [[contractible space]] of choices. Often, however, <math>\widehat{X}</math>  itself is not nilpotent but only an inverse limit of a tower of nilpotent spaces. This tower, as a pro-space, always models the homology type of the given pointed space <math>X</math>. Hence,
the Bousfield-Kan completion of a space is in precise sense the nilpotent completion of that space, with respect to a given ring. The Bousfield-Kan completion  tower  of any connected pointed space <math>{X}</math>, is a tower of nilpotent spaces which has the same (R-) pro-homology as the give space <math>{X}</math>.



Nilpotent spaces admit a good arithmetic localization theory in the sense of Bousfield and Kan cited above, and the unstable [[Adams spectral sequence]] strongly converges for any such space. 
Nilpotent spaces admit splitting by the so called arthmetic square that present any nilpotent space as a homotpy pull-back of rational and p-adic localizations. 

Nilpotent spaces apear naturally as spaces of automorphism of finite dimensional spaces. Let <math>{aut_I{X}}</math> 
be the space of pointed  homotopy self-equivalence  of  a finite dimensional  <math>{K}</math>, that induces identity on the homotopy groups up to the dimension of <math>{K}</math>.  Then the classifying space <math>Baut_I{K}</math> is a nilpotent space.

Let <math>X</math> be a nilpotent space  and let <math>h</math> be a reduced generalized homology theory, such as [[K-theory]]. If <math>h(X)=0</math>, then <math>h</math> vanishes on any Postnikov section of <math>X</math>. This follows from a theorem that states that
any such section is <math>X</math>-cellular. It is known that any cellularization functor  <math>cell_A X</math> of a truncated nilpotent space is a truncated nilpotent space. But it is conjectured by E.D. Farjoun  that the same is true for any localization <math>L_f X</math> of a  truncated nilpotent space <math> X=X_{<n}</math>.
